stimuli.title: John Locke, Second Treatise of Government (1689)
stimuli.html:
The English philosopher John Locke wrote about why people form governments. In the excerpts below, the "state of nature" means life before any government exists, and an "estate" is a person's land and possessions.

Men being, as has been said, by nature, all free, equal, and independent, no one can be put out of this estate, and subjected to the political power of another, without his own consent. The only way whereby any one divests himself of his natural liberty, and puts on the bonds of civil society, is by agreeing with other men to join and unite into a community for their comfortable, safe, and peaceable living one amongst another, in a secure enjoyment of their properties, and a greater security against any, that are not of it.

. . . the enjoyment of the property he has in this state is very unsafe, very unsecure. . . . [He] is willing to join in society with others . . . for the mutual preservation of their lives, liberties and estates, which I call by the general name, property.

The great and chief end, therefore, of men's uniting into commonwealths, and putting themselves under government, is the preservation of their property. To which in the state of nature there are many things wanting. First, There wants an established, settled, known law, received and allowed by common consent to be the standard of right and wrong, and the common measure to decide all controversies between them . . .
stimuli.source: Excerpts from John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Chapter VIII, Section 95, and Chapter IX, Sections 123–124 (published 1689)

stimuli.title: John Locke on the Lawmaking Power
stimuli.html:
Later in the same work, Locke discusses the "legislative," the body that makes the laws. A "fiduciary" power is one that is held in trust for someone else. "Reposed" means placed.

. . . yet the legislative being only a fiduciary power to act for certain ends, there remains still in the people a supreme power to remove or alter the legislative, when they find the legislative act contrary to the trust reposed in them: for all power given with trust for the attaining an end, being limited by that end, whenever that end is manifestly neglected, or opposed, the trust must necessarily be forfeited, and the power devolve into the hands of those that gave it, who may place it anew where they shall think best for their safety and security.
stimuli.source: Excerpt from John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Chapter XIII, Section 149 (published 1689)

stimuli.title: U.S. Constitution, Article II, Section 1 (excerpts)
stimuli.html:
The executive Power shall be vested in a President of the United States of America. He shall hold his Office during the Term of four Years, and, together with the Vice President, chosen for the same Term, be elected, as follows . . .

. . . No Person except a natural born Citizen, or a Citizen of the United States, at the time of the Adoption of this Constitution, shall be eligible to the Office of President; neither shall any Person be eligible to that Office who shall not have attained to the Age of thirty five Years, and been fourteen Years a Resident within the United States.
stimuli.source: Excerpts from the Constitution of the United States, Article II, Section 1 (1787)

stimuli.title: U.S. Constitution, Article II, Sections 2–4 (excerpts)
stimuli.html:
Section 2. The President shall be Commander in Chief of the Army and Navy of the United States, and of the Militia of the several States, when called into the actual Service of the United States . . .

He shall have Power, by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, to make Treaties, provided two thirds of the Senators present concur; and he shall nominate, and by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, shall appoint Ambassadors, other public Ministers and Consuls, Judges of the supreme Court, and all other Officers of the United States . . .

Section 3. He shall from time to time give to the Congress Information of the State of the Union, and recommend to their Consideration such Measures as he shall judge necessary and expedient . . . he shall take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed . . .

Section 4. The President, Vice President and all civil Officers of the United States, shall be removed from Office on Impeachment for, and Conviction of, Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors.
stimuli.source: Excerpts from the Constitution of the United States, Article II, Sections 2–4 (1787)

stimuli.title: The Fifteenth Amendment (1870)
stimuli.html:
Section 1. The right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.

Section 2. The Congress shall have power to enforce this article by appropriate legislation.
stimuli.source: Amendment XV, Constitution of the United States, ratified 1870

stimuli.title: Promise and Practice: Voting After the Fifteenth Amendment
stimuli.html:
The Fifteenth Amendment, ratified in 1870, promised that no citizen would be denied the vote because of race. In the years right after the Civil War, hundreds of thousands of Black men in the South registered and voted, and Black voters helped elect more than a dozen Black members of Congress.

After federal troops withdrew from the South in 1877, however, many Southern state governments adopted new voting rules. A poll tax required citizens to pay a fee before voting, which kept many poor citizens, Black and white, away from the polls. A literacy test required a would-be voter to read or explain a passage, often a section of the state constitution, to the satisfaction of a local registrar, who could pass or fail applicants as he chose. Some states added grandfather clauses that excused a man from these requirements if his grandfather had been eligible to vote before 1867, a time when almost no Black Southerners could vote. None of these rules mentioned race. Yet together with threats and violence, they drove Black voter registration sharply down. The Supreme Court struck down grandfather clauses in 1915, but poll taxes and literacy tests remained.

Change came in the 1960s. The Twenty-fourth Amendment, ratified in 1964, banned poll taxes in federal elections. In 1965, using the power that Section 2 of the Fifteenth Amendment gives it, Congress passed the Voting Rights Act. The law suspended literacy tests in areas with a history of low voter registration or turnout and allowed federal examiners to register voters there.
stimuli.source: Original reading written for this test

stimuli.title: Political Cartoon (described)
stimuli.html: The cartoon shows a hallway outside a door marked OFFICE OF YOUR REPRESENTATIVE. A long line of people in business suits moves through the open door. Each person carries a briefcase with a label: FARM GROUPS, LABOR UNIONS, BANKS, ENVIRONMENTAL GROUPS, RETIREES' ASSOCIATION, and TECH INDUSTRY. A smiling staff member holds the door open for them. At the far end of the hallway, a woman in work clothes, labeled CONSTITUENT, holds a single sheet of paper marked MY LETTER. A small sign taped to the wall beside her reads: YOUR CONCERNS ARE IMPORTANT TO US. PLEASE WAIT.
stimuli.source: Original cartoon description written for this test

stimuli.title: Letter to the Editor
stimuli.html:
To the Editor:

Our city council should lower the voting age for city elections to 16. Sixteen-year-olds are mature enough to make thoughtful choices about the issues that shape their lives. The Twenty-sixth Amendment, ratified in 1971, protects the right of citizens 18 years of age or older to vote. Voting is a habit, and people who start young will keep voting all their lives. Lowering the voting age is the most important step our council could take to strengthen our community. The council should hold a public hearing on this proposal before the end of the year.

— A high school teacher
stimuli.source: Original letter written for this test

stimuli.title: The Declaration of Sentiments (1848)
stimuli.html:
In July 1848, about 300 people gathered in Seneca Falls, New York, for the first women's rights convention in the United States. One hundred of them, 68 women and 32 men, signed the Declaration of Sentiments, written mainly by Elizabeth Cady Stanton. Excerpts follow.

We hold these truths to be self-evident: that all men and women are created equal; that they are endowed by their Creator with certain inalienable rights; that among these are life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness; that to secure these rights governments are instituted, deriving their just powers from the consent of the governed. . . .

The history of mankind is a history of repeated injuries and usurpations on the part of man toward woman, having in direct object the establishment of an absolute tyranny over her. . . .

He has never permitted her to exercise her inalienable right to the elective franchise.

He has compelled her to submit to laws, in the formation of which she had no voice. . . .

He has made her, if married, in the eye of the law, civilly dead.

He has taken from her all right in property, even to the wages she earns. . . .

He has denied her the facilities for obtaining a thorough education, all colleges being closed against her.
stimuli.source: Excerpts from the Declaration of Sentiments, Seneca Falls Convention, Seneca Falls, New York, July 1848

stimuli.title: Second Inaugural Address (1865)
stimuli.html:
President Abraham Lincoln delivered his Second Inaugural Address on March 4, 1865, as the Civil War neared its end. In the excerpts, "parties" means the two sides in the conflict, and "the insurgents" means the rebels of the Confederacy.

. . . Both parties deprecated war, but one of them would make war rather than let the nation survive, and the other would accept war rather than let it perish, and the war came.

One-eighth of the whole population were colored slaves, not distributed generally over the Union, but localized in the southern part of it. These slaves constituted a peculiar and powerful interest. All knew that this interest was somehow the cause of the war. To strengthen, perpetuate, and extend this interest was the object for which the insurgents would rend the Union even by war, while the Government claimed no right to do more than to restrict the territorial enlargement of it. Neither party expected for the war the magnitude or the duration which it has already attained. Neither anticipated that the cause of the conflict might cease with or even before the conflict itself should cease. . . .
stimuli.source: Excerpts from President Abraham Lincoln's Second Inaugural Address, March 4, 1865. (Word help: "deprecated" = disapproved of; "peculiar" = special or distinctive; "perpetuate" = make last; "rend" = tear apart; "magnitude" = size.)

stimuli.title: The Fourteen Points (1918)
stimuli.html:
On January 8, 1918, about nine months after the United States entered World War I, President Woodrow Wilson spoke before both houses of Congress and proposed fourteen points as the basis for a lasting peace. Four of the points are excerpted below.

I. Open covenants of peace, openly arrived at, after which there shall be no private international understandings of any kind but diplomacy shall proceed always frankly and in the public view.

III. The removal, so far as possible, of all economic barriers and the establishment of an equality of trade conditions among all the nations consenting to the peace and associating themselves for its maintenance.

IV. Adequate guarantees given and taken that national armaments will be reduced to the lowest point consistent with domestic safety.

XIV. A general association of nations must be formed under specific covenants for the purpose of affording mutual guarantees of political independence and territorial integrity to great and small states alike.
stimuli.source: Excerpts from President Woodrow Wilson's address to Congress, January 8, 1918. (A "covenant" is a formal agreement.)

stimuli.title: Where Does Your Deposit Go?
stimuli.html:
When you deposit money in a bank, the bank does not simply lock all of it in a vault. Banks earn most of their income by lending. A bank keeps a fraction of its deposits as reserves, either as cash in its vault or as money in its own account at the Federal Reserve, and lends out the rest to people who want to buy cars or homes or start businesses. Borrowers pay interest on their loans, and the bank uses part of that interest to pay interest to its depositors. This system is called fractional reserve banking.

For example, suppose a bank keeps 10 percent of every deposit in reserve. When a customer deposits $1,000, the bank holds $100 and can lend the other $900.

Fractional reserve banking works well as long as only a small share of depositors want their money back on any given day. But if many depositors fear that a bank is in trouble and rush to withdraw their money at the same time, an event called a bank run, the bank may not have enough cash on hand to pay them all. In the early 1930s, waves of bank runs swept the country, thousands of banks failed, and many depositors lost their savings.

In response, Congress passed the Banking Act of 1933, which created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC). Deposit insurance took effect on January 1, 1934. Today the FDIC insures deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each account ownership category. Because depositors know their insured money is safe even if a bank fails, they have far less reason to start a run.
stimuli.source: Original reading written for this test

stimuli.title: The Federal Reserve System
stimuli.html:
Congress created the Federal Reserve, the central bank of the United States, through the Federal Reserve Act, which President Woodrow Wilson signed in December 1913. The system has three main parts:

  • The Board of Governors in Washington, D.C., has seven members. Each is nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate for a term of 14 years. The terms are staggered so that one term ends every two years.
  • Twelve regional Federal Reserve Banks, in cities such as Boston, Chicago, and San Francisco, serve the banks in their districts.
  • The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), made up of the seven governors and five of the regional bank presidents, sets the direction of monetary policy.

Because governors serve long terms and can be removed only "for cause," not simply for disagreeing with the President, the Federal Reserve can make decisions that may be unpopular in the short run, such as raising interest rates to slow rising prices, without worrying about the next election. Congress still oversees the system, and the chair of the Board reports to Congress twice a year.

One of the Federal Reserve's main tools is open market operations, the buying and selling of U.S. government securities (bonds). When the Federal Reserve buys securities, it pays by adding money to banks' reserve accounts, so banks have more money to lend and interest rates tend to fall. When it sells securities, bank reserves shrink and interest rates tend to rise. The Federal Reserve also acts as a lender of last resort: during a crisis, a sound bank that is short of cash can borrow from the Federal Reserve instead of failing.
stimuli.source: Original reading written for this test

stimuli.title: The Dust Bowl
stimuli.html:
Before settlers arrived, the southern Great Plains, including parts of Kansas, Colorado, New Mexico, Oklahoma, and Texas, were covered by grasses whose deep, tangled roots held the soil in place through droughts and strong winds. In the late 1800s and early 1900s, farmers began plowing this grassland to plant wheat. When wheat prices climbed during World War I and new gasoline-powered tractors made plowing faster, millions more acres were turned over. When wheat prices fell in the 1920s, many farmers plowed even more land to make up for their lower income.

Then, in the early 1930s, a severe drought struck. Crops withered, and the bare, dry soil had nothing to hold it down. Strong winds lifted the topsoil into enormous dust storms. On April 14, 1935, a day remembered as "Black Sunday," a towering wall of dust rolled across the Plains and turned day into night. Dust drifted against fences and houses, buried farm equipment, killed livestock, and caused breathing illnesses that people called "dust pneumonia."

The federal government responded. In 1935 Congress created the Soil Conservation Service, which taught farmers new methods, and the government paid many farmers to adopt them. Contour plowing, plowing across a slope instead of up and down it, kept soil and rainwater from running off. Farmers rotated crops and left crop stubble in their fields to protect the ground. A federal program also planted long rows of trees, called shelterbelts, from North Dakota to Texas to break the force of the wind. When rains returned at the end of the decade, these practices helped the land recover.
stimuli.source: Original reading written for this test

stimuli.title: Leaving the Plains
stimuli.html:
The table shows population and farm data for Prairie County, a farming county on the southern Plains.

YearPopulationNumber of farms
193012,5002,100
193510,9001,850
19408,0001,300

During the 1930s, hundreds of thousands of people left the Great Plains and nearby states. Many traveled west on Route 66 toward California. Families left for many reasons. Years of crop failure left farmers with no income, and banks foreclosed on farms when owners could not repay their loans. Many tenant farmers, who rented land instead of owning it, were forced off when landowners bought tractors that let one family farm land once worked by several. At the same time, word spread of jobs harvesting fruit, vegetables, and cotton in California's farm valleys, where the growing season is long.

Many migrants found far more workers than jobs when they arrived. Wages were low, and many families lived in roadside camps. Not all of the migrants came from the Dust Bowl itself. Many came from parts of Oklahoma, Arkansas, Texas, and Missouri that were hurt by drought and the Great Depression rather than by dust storms.
stimuli.source: Prairie County data created for this test; original reading written for this test

items.skill: Civics: natural rights and the social contract
items.prompt: Which statement best summarizes Locke's main idea in the excerpts?
options: People give up some of their natural freedom and agree to form a government mainly so that their lives, liberties, and estates will be better protected.
Rulers receive their authority directly from God, so people must obey them whether or not they agree.
People in the state of nature are completely safe, so government exists mainly to collect taxes.
The main purpose of government is to divide all property equally among the people.
items.explain: Locke says people are "by nature, all free, equal, and independent" and join a community only "by agreeing with other men" (consent). He gives the reason: "The great and chief end . . . of men's uniting into commonwealths . . . is the preservation of their property," which he defines as "lives, liberties and estates." The idea that rulers get power directly from God (divine right) is the view Locke argued against, and he says life in the state of nature is "very unsafe," not completely safe.

items.skill: Civics: vocabulary in a primary source
items.prompt: Locke uses the word property in a broader way than most people do today. According to the excerpts, what does Locke include in "property"?
options: Only land and the buildings on it
People's lives, liberties, and estates
Only money and goods that can be bought and sold
Land owned in common by the government
items.explain: Locke states that people unite "for the mutual preservation of their lives, liberties and estates, which I call by the general name, property." So his "property" covers life and liberty as well as possessions. Land and buildings (an estate) are only one part of what he means.

items.prompt: Locke says that in the state of nature "There wants an established, settled, known law . . . to be the standard of right and wrong." Which feature of American government most directly addresses this problem?
options: Allowing each person to decide for himself or herself what is right and wrong
Giving a single ruler unlimited power to settle every dispute
Requiring laws to be written down, made public, and applied equally to everyone
Electing the President to a four-year term
items.explain: "Wants" here means "lacks." Locke's complaint is that there is no settled, known law that everyone accepts. The rule of law, with written, published laws that apply to everyone, including leaders, solves that problem. Letting each person decide right and wrong is the state of nature Locke describes as unsafe, and a ruler with unlimited power would not give people a "known law" made by "common consent." Presidential elections are about choosing leaders, not about having known laws.

items.prompt: Locke argues that lawmaking power is held "in trust" and can be taken back by "those that gave it." Which feature of the U.S. political system most closely reflects this idea?
options: Federal judges hold their offices for life, as long as they show good behavior.
Before 1913, U.S. senators were chosen by state legislatures rather than by voters.
The President can veto bills passed by Congress.
Voters can defeat members of Congress in regular elections and replace them with new lawmakers.
items.explain: Locke says the people keep "a supreme power to remove or alter the legislative" when lawmakers betray their trust, and the power returns to "those that gave it, who may place it anew." In the United States, voters give lawmakers their power and can take it back by voting them out and choosing someone new. Lifetime terms for judges and senators chosen by legislatures both keep officials away from direct removal by the people. A veto is one branch checking another, not the people taking back power.

items.prompt: Based on the excerpt from Article II, which of these people are eligible to serve as President? Select two answers.
options: A 38-year-old born in Ohio who has lived in the United States her entire life
A 52-year-old born in another country who moved to the United States at age 10 and became a naturalized citizen at age 20
A 34-year-old born in Texas who has lived in the United States his entire life
A 61-year-old born in Georgia who has lived in the United States for the past 40 years
A 45-year-old born in California who moved abroad as an infant and returned to live in the United States 9 years ago
items.explain:
Article II sets three requirements: (1) a natural born citizen, (2) at least 35 years old, and (3) a resident of the United States for at least 14 years.

  • The 38-year-old born in Ohio meets all three. Eligible.
  • The 61-year-old born in Georgia with 40 years of residence meets all three. Eligible.
  • The naturalized citizen is not natural born. (The exception for people who were citizens "at the time of the Adoption of this Constitution" applied only to the founding generation.) Not eligible.
  • The 34-year-old is under 35. Not eligible.
  • The 45-year-old has lived in the United States only about 9 years, fewer than 14. Not eligible.

items.prompt: Article II sets a four-year term for the President but does not limit how many terms a President may serve. Which development later added such a limit?
options: A law passed by Congress in 1913 that limited Presidents to two terms
The Twenty-second Amendment, ratified in 1951, which says no person may be elected President more than twice
The Twelfth Amendment, which requires electors to cast separate votes for President and Vice President
The Supreme Court's decision in Marbury v. Madison
items.explain: After Franklin D. Roosevelt was elected four times, Congress proposed and the states ratified the Twenty-second Amendment (1951), which says no person shall be elected President more than twice. Because the term of office is set by the Constitution, an ordinary law could not change it; an amendment was needed. The Twelfth Amendment changed how electors vote, not how many terms a President may serve, and Marbury v. Madison established judicial review.

items.prompt: Some presidential powers in Article II can be used by the President alone. Others require the Senate's "Advice and Consent." Drag each power into the correct category.
choices: Serve as Commander in Chief of the armed forces
Appoint justices of the Supreme Court
Give Congress information on the State of the Union
Take care that the laws are faithfully executed
bins: President with the Senate's advice and consent
items.explain:
President alone: serving as Commander in Chief, reporting on the State of the Union, and taking care that the laws are faithfully executed. The excerpt places no Senate approval requirement on these duties.

With the Senate's advice and consent: making treaties (two-thirds of senators present must agree) and appointing ambassadors and Supreme Court justices. The excerpt says the President makes these "by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate." A common mistake is placing appointments under "President alone" because the President picks the nominee; the Senate must still confirm.

items.prompt: Suppose 94 senators are present when the Senate votes on a treaty. Based on Article II, what is the smallest number of senators who must vote in favor for the treaty to be approved?
items.explain:
Article II requires that "two thirds of the Senators present concur."
2/3 × 94 = 188 ÷ 3 = 62.67 (rounded).
A vote of 62 is not enough, because 62 ÷ 94 ≈ 0.660, which is less than two-thirds.
A vote of 63 is enough, because 63 ÷ 94 ≈ 0.670, which is at least two-thirds.
The smallest number is 63. A common error is using all 100 senators (which would give 67) instead of the 94 who are present.

items.prompt: A President nominates a person to serve as a federal judge, but the Senate votes against confirming the nominee. Which statement best describes what happened?
options: The judicial branch checked the power of the legislative branch.
A state government used one of its reserved powers.
The President used a veto to block an action by the Senate.
The legislative branch checked the appointment power of the executive branch.
items.explain: Under Article II, the President "shall nominate, and by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, shall appoint . . . Judges." The Senate is part of Congress, the legislative branch. By rejecting the nominee, it checked the executive branch. This is an example of checks and balances. The courts were not involved, states have no role in confirming federal judges, and a veto is the President's check on bills, not on Senate votes.

items.prompt: Section 4 says the President "shall be removed from Office on Impeachment for, and Conviction of" certain offenses. Based on the excerpt and your knowledge of the Constitution, which statement about this process is accurate?
options: The House of Representatives may impeach (formally charge) the President, but removal requires conviction by two-thirds of the senators present.
Voters may remove a President at any time by signing a national petition.
The Supreme Court may remove a President whose policies it considers unwise.
A President is removed from office as soon as a majority of the House votes to impeach.
items.explain: Section 4 requires both impeachment and conviction. Under Article I, the House has the sole power to impeach (bring charges), and the Senate holds the trial; conviction requires two-thirds of the senators present. Impeachment by the House alone does not remove a President: several Presidents have been impeached and then acquitted by the Senate. The grounds are "Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors," not disagreement with policies, and there is no national petition process.

items.prompt: Suppose that in 1880 a state passed a law stating that no person who had once been enslaved could vote in state elections. How would this law be judged under the Fifteenth Amendment?
options: It would be allowed, because the amendment applies only to the federal government.
It would be allowed, because states have the reserved power to set all voting rules.
It would violate the amendment, because it denies the vote "on account of . . . previous condition of servitude."
It would violate the amendment, because the amendment guarantees the right to vote to every adult.
items.explain: Section 1 says the right to vote "shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude." "Previous condition of servitude" means having once been enslaved, so this law is exactly what the amendment forbids. The amendment applies to states as well as to the federal government. It does not guarantee the vote to every adult; for example, it said nothing about sex, and women were not guaranteed the vote until the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920.

items.prompt: Grandfather clauses did not mention race. Based on the reading, how did a grandfather clause tied to the year 1867 still work to keep Black Southerners from voting?
options: It required Black citizens, but not white citizens, to pay a poll tax twice.
Because almost no Black Southerners could vote before 1867, few Black men could use the exemption from poll taxes and literacy tests, while many white men could.
It applied only to federal elections, so states could still deny the vote in state elections.
The year 1867 was when the Fifteenth Amendment was ratified, so the clause canceled the amendment.
items.explain: The reading says grandfather clauses "excused a man from these requirements if his grandfather had been eligible to vote before 1867, a time when almost no Black Southerners could vote." Most white men could claim the exemption, but almost no Black men could, so Black citizens still faced poll taxes and literacy tests. The rule never mentioned race, but its effect fell along racial lines. The Fifteenth Amendment was ratified in 1870, not 1867, and the reading says nothing about the clauses applying only to federal elections or doubling a tax.

items.prompt:
Complete the statement.

Section 2 of the Fifteenth Amendment gives {{0}} the power to enforce the amendment. Using that power, Congress passed the {{1}}, which suspended literacy tests in areas with a history of low voter registration or turnout.

options: the Supreme Court
Congress
the state legislatures
the President alone
Twenty-fourth Amendment
Emancipation Proclamation
Voting Rights Act of 1965
Federal Reserve Act

items.explain:
Blank 1: Congress. Section 2 reads, "The Congress shall have power to enforce this article by appropriate legislation."

Blank 2: Voting Rights Act of 1965. The reading says that in 1965, using this power, Congress passed the Voting Rights Act, which "suspended literacy tests" and sent federal examiners to register voters. The Twenty-fourth Amendment is a tempting choice, but it banned poll taxes in federal elections, not literacy tests, and it is an amendment ratified by the states rather than a law passed by Congress.

items.skill: Civics: interpreting data in a table
items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data in the table?
options: In March 1965, more than half of voting-age Black residents were registered in every state shown.
In 1988, Black voter registration was higher in Georgia than in Louisiana.
Black voter registration fell in South Carolina after the Voting Rights Act.
Black voter registration rose in every state shown, and the largest increase was in Mississippi.
items.explain:
Find each increase (1988 minus 1965):
Alabama: 68.4 − 19.3 = 49.1
Georgia: 56.8 − 27.4 = 29.4
Louisiana: 77.1 − 31.6 = 45.5
Mississippi: 74.2 − 6.7 = 67.5
South Carolina: 56.7 − 37.3 = 19.4
Every state rose, and Mississippi's gain (67.5 points) was the largest. In 1965 no state shown was above 50 percent (the highest was South Carolina at 37.3), Georgia (56.8) was below Louisiana (77.1) in 1988, and South Carolina rose rather than fell.

items.prompt: By how many percentage points did Black voter registration in Alabama increase from March 1965 to November 1988?
items.explain:
Alabama, November 1988: 68.4 percent.
Alabama, March 1965: 19.3 percent.
68.4 − 19.3 = 49.1 percentage points.
A common error is reading the wrong row (for example, Mississippi's increase of 67.5 points) or adding the two values.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the cartoonist's point of view?
options: Organized interest groups often get more of lawmakers' attention than individual citizens do.
Interest groups from only one side of politics have influence in Congress.
Lawmakers refuse to read any letters from the people they represent.
Citizens should stop contacting their representatives because it is a waste of time.
items.explain: The cartoon shows a long line of groups with briefcases being welcomed through the door while a single constituent with "MY LETTER" waits at the far end under a sign that says "PLEASE WAIT." The contrast suggests that organized groups get easier access to lawmakers than individual citizens. The labels include groups across the political spectrum (labor unions and banks, environmental groups and the tech industry), so the cartoon is not about one side. It exaggerates the wait but does not show lawmakers refusing all letters, and it does not tell citizens to give up.

items.prompt: Click the sentence from the letter that states a fact that can be checked, rather than an opinion.
spans: Our city council should lower the voting age for city elections to 16.
Sixteen-year-olds are mature enough to make thoughtful choices about the issues that shape their lives.
The Twenty-sixth Amendment, ratified in 1971, protects the right of citizens 18 years of age or older to vote.
Voting is a habit, and people who start young will keep voting all their lives.
Lowering the voting age is the most important step our council could take to strengthen our community.
The council should hold a public hearing on this proposal before the end of the year.
items.explain: The sentence about the Twenty-sixth Amendment can be verified by reading the Constitution: it was ratified in 1971 and protects the voting rights of citizens 18 and older. Every other sentence is a judgment or recommendation. Words such as "should," "mature enough," and "most important" signal opinions, and "people who start young will keep voting all their lives" is a prediction the writer does not support with evidence.

items.prompt: Which piece of evidence, if accurate, would most strengthen the letter writer's argument?
options: A survey showing that most adults in the city oppose lowering the voting age
A report that the city's population grew by 3 percent last year
A study finding that people who vote in the first election they are eligible for are more likely to keep voting in later elections
A list of the dates of the next three city council meetings
items.explain: The writer claims that "Voting is a habit, and people who start young will keep voting all their lives," but gives no evidence. A study showing that voting in one's first eligible election predicts voting later would directly support that claim. A survey showing adult opposition would weaken the argument, and population growth and meeting dates are not related to whether 16-year-olds should vote.

items.prompt: The opening of the Declaration of Sentiments closely follows the Declaration of Independence (1776) but says that "all men and women are created equal." What was the most likely purpose of this choice?
options: To declare that women in the United States were forming a separate nation
To argue that the nation's founding principles should apply to women as fully as to men
To show that the Declaration of Independence had already given women the right to vote
To ask Great Britain to protect the rights of American women
items.explain: By borrowing the famous words of 1776 and adding "and women," the authors claimed that the same self-evident truths, natural rights, and consent of the governed that justified American independence also applied to women. The document goes on to list the rights women were denied, including the vote, so it does not claim women already had that right. It called for equal rights within the United States, not a new nation or British protection.

items.prompt: The Nineteenth Amendment, ratified in 1920, says the right to vote cannot be denied "on account of sex." Click the sentence from the Declaration of Sentiments that names the grievance this amendment most directly addressed.
spans: We hold these truths to be self-evident: that all men and women are created equal; that they are endowed by their Creator with certain inalienable rights; that among these are life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness; that to secure these rights governments are instituted, deriving their just powers from the consent of the governed.
The history of mankind is a history of repeated injuries and usurpations on the part of man toward woman, having in direct object the establishment of an absolute tyranny over her.
He has never permitted her to exercise her inalienable right to the elective franchise.
He has made her, if married, in the eye of the law, civilly dead.
He has taken from her all right in property, even to the wages she earns.
He has denied her the facilities for obtaining a thorough education, all colleges being closed against her.
items.explain: The "elective franchise" is the right to vote. The grievance that women were never permitted "to exercise her inalienable right to the elective franchise" was resolved for the nation when the Nineteenth Amendment barred denying the vote on account of sex, 72 years after Seneca Falls. The other grievances concern married women's legal status, property and wages, and education, which were changed through other laws over time, not by the Nineteenth Amendment.

items.skill: U.S. history: causes of the Civil War
items.prompt: According to Lincoln, how did the goals of "the insurgents" and of the national government differ regarding slavery before the war?
options: The insurgents wanted to strengthen and extend slavery, while the government claimed only the right to keep it from spreading into new territories.
The government planned to end slavery at once in every state, while the insurgents wanted only to limit its spread.
Both sides agreed that slavery should be ended slowly, but they disagreed about the national budget.
The insurgents wanted to end slavery, while the government wanted to protect it.
items.explain: Lincoln says that "To strengthen, perpetuate, and extend this interest" (slavery) "was the object for which the insurgents would rend the Union even by war, while the Government claimed no right to do more than to restrict the territorial enlargement of it." "Territorial enlargement" means spreading into the western territories. The government did not claim the power to end slavery at once in the states where it already existed, so the second choice reverses Lincoln's description.

items.skill: U.S. history: point of view in a primary source
items.prompt: Which statement best describes Lincoln's point of view, in the first paragraph of the excerpt, about how the war began?
options: The North started the war in order to end slavery in the Southern states.
Both sides were equally eager to go to war and equally responsible for it.
War could have been avoided if the national government had agreed to expand slavery.
Although both sides disliked war, one side chose war to break up the Union, while the other accepted war only to preserve it.
items.explain: Lincoln says "Both parties deprecated war" (both disapproved of it), "but one of them would make war rather than let the nation survive" (the Confederacy, which seceded), "and the other would accept war rather than let it perish" (the Union). He presents the Union as accepting war to save the nation, not as starting it to end slavery, and he does not describe the two sides as equally eager. Nothing in the excerpt suggests he thought the government should have agreed to expand slavery; the next paragraph says the government sought to restrict it.

items.prompt: Which organization grew most directly out of Point XIV of Wilson's plan?
options: The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO)
The Warsaw Pact
The League of Nations
The Federal Reserve System
items.explain: Point XIV calls for "A general association of nations" to guarantee the "political independence and territorial integrity" of all states. This became the League of Nations, created by the peace settlement after World War I. NATO (1949) and the Warsaw Pact (1955) were Cold War military alliances formed decades later, and the Federal Reserve is the U.S. central bank, created in 1913.

items.skill: U.S. history: World War I and the treaty power
items.prompt:
Complete the statement.

In Point I, Wilson called for open diplomacy because many people believed that {{0}} had helped drag nations into World War I. At home, Wilson's peace plan faced a constitutional hurdle: a treaty needs the approval of {{1}}. The Senate did not approve the Treaty of Versailles, and the United States never joined the League of Nations.

options: secret alliances and private agreements
freedom of navigation on the seas
the removal of trade barriers
the reduction of national armaments
a simple majority of the House of Representatives
two-thirds of the senators present
the Supreme Court
three-fourths of the states

items.explain:
Blank 1: secret alliances and private agreements. Point I rejects "private international understandings of any kind" in favor of diplomacy "in the public view." Before 1914, a web of alliances, some with secret terms, pulled one nation after another into the war. The other choices are goals Wilson supported (Points II, III, and IV), not problems he blamed for the war.

Blank 2: two-thirds of the senators present. Article II says the President makes treaties "by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate . . . provided two thirds of the Senators present concur." The House plays no role in approving treaties, and three-fourths of the states is the requirement for ratifying constitutional amendments.

items.prompt: Drag each event into the order in which it happened, from earliest (1st) to latest (5th).
choices: President Wilson presents the Fourteen Points to Congress.
The Seneca Falls Convention issues the Declaration of Sentiments.
President Lincoln delivers his Second Inaugural Address.
items.explain: Correct order: (1) Seneca Falls Convention, 1848; (2) Lincoln's Second Inaugural Address, March 1865; (3) Fifteenth Amendment ratified, 1870; (4) Fourteen Points, January 1918; (5) Nineteenth Amendment ratified, 1920. A common mistake is placing the Nineteenth Amendment before the Fourteen Points; women won the national right to vote only after World War I ended.

items.prompt: A customer deposits $8,000 in a bank that keeps 10 percent of every deposit in reserve, as in the reading's example. What is the greatest amount of this deposit that the bank can lend? Enter the amount in dollars.
items.explain:
Reserve the bank must hold: 10% of $8,000 = 0.10 × 8,000 = $800.
Amount available to lend: $8,000 − $800 = $7,200.
A common error is entering the reserve ($800) instead of the amount that can be lent.

items.prompt: According to the reading, why can a bank run cause even a well-run bank to fail?
options: Because the bank has lent out most of its deposits, it does not keep enough cash on hand to repay all of its depositors at once.
Because the Federal Reserve requires banks to close whenever depositors withdraw money.
Because banks are not allowed to charge interest on the loans they make.
Because deposit insurance pays depositors only if the bank stays open.
items.explain: Under fractional reserve banking, a bank keeps only a fraction of deposits as reserves and "lends out the rest." That works when only a few depositors withdraw on a given day, but in a run "the bank may not have enough cash on hand to pay them all." The reading says banks earn interest on loans, and FDIC insurance protects depositors precisely when a bank fails.

items.prompt: Based on the reading, what is the main reason members of the Board of Governors serve long, staggered 14-year terms?
options: To make sure each President can replace the entire Board during a single term
To allow the Federal Reserve to make decisions that may be unpopular in the short run without pressure from upcoming elections
To give the twelve regional banks complete control over monetary policy
To prevent Congress from overseeing the Federal Reserve
items.explain: The reading explains that because governors "serve long terms and can be removed only 'for cause,'" the Federal Reserve can take unpopular steps, such as raising interest rates to slow rising prices, "without worrying about the next election." Staggering means only one term ends every two years, so a single four-year presidential term would normally fill only about two of the seven seats, not the entire Board. The reading also says Congress still oversees the system.

items.prompt:
Complete the statement.

During an economic slowdown, the Federal Reserve wants to make borrowing cheaper so that businesses and households will spend more. Using open market operations, it would {{0}} government securities. This {{1}} the reserves that banks have available to lend, so interest rates tend to {{2}}.

options: sell
buy
cancel
decreases
does not change
increases
rise
fall
stay the same

items.explain: The reading says that when the Federal Reserve buys securities, "it pays by adding money to banks' reserve accounts, so banks have more money to lend and interest rates tend to fall." So the Fed would buy securities, which increases bank reserves, and interest rates tend to fall. Selling securities does the opposite: reserves shrink and rates rise, which is used to slow the economy and rising prices.

items.prompt: Which conclusions are supported by the graph and the information above it? Select two answers.
options: The number of bank suspensions was highest in 1933.
The number of bank suspensions rose every year from 1929 to 1933.
Bank suspensions dropped sharply in the first year that federal deposit insurance was in effect.
Fewer than 1,000 banks suspended operations in 1930, 1931, and 1932 combined.
Federal deposit insurance took effect before the number of suspensions began to rise.
items.explain: The tallest bar is 1933, about 4,000 suspensions. Deposit insurance took effect January 1, 1934, and suspensions fell from about 4,000 in 1933 to about 60 in 1934. Suspensions did not rise every year: they fell from about 2,290 in 1931 to about 1,450 in 1932. The 1930–1932 total is about 1,350 + 2,290 + 1,450 = 5,090, far more than 1,000. Insurance began in 1934, after the rise, not before it.

items.prompt: According to the reading, which human action did the most to make the southern Plains vulnerable to the dust storms of the 1930s?
options: Planting long rows of trees called shelterbelts
The severe drought of the early 1930s
Rotating crops and leaving stubble in the fields
Plowing up native grasses whose roots had held the soil in place
items.explain: The reading explains that native grasses' "deep, tangled roots held the soil in place," and that farmers plowed millions of acres of this grassland to plant wheat. When drought killed the crops, "the bare, dry soil had nothing to hold it down." The drought was a cause, but it was a natural event, not a human action. Shelterbelts, crop rotation, and leaving stubble were responses that reduced erosion.

items.prompt: Contour plowing and shelterbelts were both intended to
options: increase the number of acres planted in wheat
help farm families move to California
keep soil from being carried away by wind and water
raise the price farmers received for wheat
items.explain: The reading says contour plowing "kept soil and rainwater from running off," and shelterbelts were planted "to break the force of the wind." Both protect the soil from erosion. Neither practice was meant to expand wheat planting, which had helped cause the problem, or to change prices or move families.

items.prompt: By about what percent did the population of Prairie County decrease from 1930 to 1940?
items.explain:
Decrease: 12,500 − 8,000 = 4,500 people.
Percent decrease = decrease ÷ original value = 4,500 ÷ 12,500 = 0.36 = 36%.
Dividing by the 1940 population instead (4,500 ÷ 8,000 ≈ 56%) is a common error, and 64% (8,000 ÷ 12,500) is the share of the population that remained.

items.prompt: A push factor drives people away from a place, and a pull factor attracts them to a new place. Based on the reading, which was a pull factor for migrants in the 1930s?
options: Banks foreclosing on farms whose owners could not repay their loans
Landowners replacing tenant farmers with tractors
Years of crop failure that left farmers with no income
Reports of jobs harvesting fruit, vegetables, and cotton in California
items.explain: Word of harvest jobs in California's farm valleys drew migrants toward a new place, so it is a pull factor. Foreclosures, tractors replacing tenant farmers, and crop failures all drove people away from the Plains, so they are push factors.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the table and the reading?
options: Prairie County grew during the 1930s because new farms were opening on cheap land.
Prairie County lost both people and farms during the 1930s, a pattern consistent with families being pushed off the land by crop failure, foreclosure, and the spread of tractors.
Every person who left the southern Plains in the 1930s left because of dust storms alone.
Most migrants who reached California quickly found steady, well-paid work.
items.explain: The table shows population falling from 12,500 to 8,000 and farms falling from 2,100 to 1,300 between 1930 and 1940. The reading explains that crop failure, foreclosures, and tractors that let one family farm land "once worked by several" forced families off farms, which fits fewer, larger farms and fewer people. The county did not grow. The reading says many migrants were hurt by drought and the Depression "rather than by dust storms," so "dust storms alone" is too broad, and it says migrants found "far more workers than jobs" and low wages.
